public_rationale: Marcus reported what a new study found. GovInfoSecurity (ISMG) covered the same study, citing researchers from Elloe AI, Stanford, MIT, CMU, ITU Copenhagen and Nvidia. It reports that the study analyzed 847 agent deployments across healthcare, finance, customer service and software development, and that 91% of tested deployments were susceptible to tool-chaining attacks. A Chinese financial outlet gives the same 847 and 91% figures. No source gives different numbers. The paper itself could not be found, so the support rests on news reports of its findings. This checks whether Marcus reported the study accurately, not whether the study's methods are sound.
limitations: Rests on news reports, not the primary paper, which was not found online.
The study's methods and how it defined 'vulnerable' could not be checked.
The Wallstreetcn report cites Marcus and may not be fully independent.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: A new study found 91% of 847 autonomous agent deployments were vulnerable to tool-chaining attacks.

statement.excerpt: A new study from researchers from Stanford, MIT CSAIL, Carnegie Mellon, ITU Copenhagen, and NVIDIA and Elloe AI Labs, examining 847 autonomous agent deployments drawn from healthcare, finance, customer service and code-generation, showed that 91% were vulnerable to subtle but dangerous tool-chaining attacks (see diagram below),
statement.document_title: Breaking: Autonomous Agents are a Shitshow

from_speaker: Stanford, MIT CSAIL, Carnegie Mellon, ITU Copenhagen, and NVIDIA and Elloe AI Labs
healthcare, finance, customer service and code-generation
91% were vulnerable to subtle but dangerous tool-chaining attacks
our_interpretation: This claim reports what a study found. It is not a claim that 91% of all real-world agents are vulnerable. It holds if the cited study reported that about 91% of 847 deployments in those sectors were susceptible to tool-chaining attacks.
No link to the paper was given and the primary text could not be found. A reputable report on the paper's findings, especially one quoting its author, counts as evidence of what the paper reported.
criteria.support_condition: The study, or a reliable report of it, says that it examined 847 agent deployments in healthcare, finance, customer service and code generation, and that 91% were susceptible to tool-chaining attacks.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The study, or a reliable report of it, gives a materially different sample size or rate, or reports no such tool-chaining figure.

evidence.excerpt: The succession of events creates tool-chaining vulnerabilities: sequences of individually permitted actions that collectively produce outcomes no single access control would allow. Ninety-one percent of tested deployments were susceptible.
evidence.explanation: Reports the study's finding that 91% of tested deployments were susceptible to tool-chaining attacks, which matches the claim.
